title: Ferrimagnetism
short_intro: Ferrimagnetism is a form of magnetism observed in materials whose neighboring magnetic moments point in opposite directions and are of unequal magnitude, resulting in a net spontaneous magnetization. These materials, typically ferrites, combine high electrical resistivity with permanent magnetic ordering.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic definition of ferrimagnetic materials, distinction between ferro-, ferri-, and antiferro-magnets, Curie-Weiss law modification, and standard examples like magnetite (Fe3O4).
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Néel's theory of ferrimagnetism involving two sublattices (A and B), molecular field equations, inverse susceptibility above the Néel temperature, and temperature dependence of spontaneous magnetization.

prerequisites: Atomic magnetic moments and Hund's rules
Exchange interaction and Weiss molecular field theory

concept_notes.heading: Microscopic Origin of Ferrimagnetism
bullets: Ferrimagnetic materials contain magnetic ions distributed over at least two different crystallographic sublattices, designated as sublattice A and sublattice B.
The exchange interaction between ions on sublattice A and sublattice B is negative (antiferromagnetic coupling), leading to antiparallel alignment of their magnetic moments.
Because the magnetic moments on the two sublattices are unequal in magnitude or number per unit volume, complete cancellation does not occur, leaving a net spontaneous magnetization.

concept_notes.heading: Magnetic Structure of Ferrites
bullets: Common ferrimagnetic oxides are spinels with the general chemical formula MO.Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, where M is a divalent metal ion such as Fe<sup>2+</sup>, Co<sup>2+</sup>, Ni<sup>2+</sup>, or Mn<sup>2+</sup>.
In the spinel lattice, metal ions occupy tetrahedral (A) and octahedral (B) interstitial sites formed by oxygen anions.
The super-exchange interaction occurs via intermediate oxygen ions, producing strong antiparallel coupling between the A and B sites.

concept_notes.heading: Temperature Dependence and Néel Temperature
bullets: Like ferromagnets, ferrimagnets possess a critical temperature called the Néel temperature (T<sub>N</sub>) or ferrimagnetic Curie temperature, above which thermal agitation destroys the ordered state, rendering the material paramagnetic.
Below T<sub>N</sub>, thermal fluctuations reduce the net spontaneous magnetization until it vanishes completely at T = T<sub>N</sub>.
In certain ferrimagnets, the temperature dependence of the two sublattice magnetizations can lead to a 'compensation point' where the net magnetization momentarily drops to zero.

concept_notes.heading: Magnetic Susceptibility Above the Néel Temperature
bullets: In the paramagnetic region (T > T<sub>N</sub>), the reciprocal magnetic susceptibility does not follow a simple Curie-Weiss law.
The inverse susceptibility vs. temperature curve exhibits a hyperbolic asymptote due to the negative inter-sublattice molecular field coefficients.
The high-temperature behavior is described by 1/χ = (T/C) - [θ/ (T - θ')] or similar modified hyperbolic relations derived from molecular field theory.

derivations.title: Molecular Field Theory of Ferrimagnetism (Two-Sublattice Model)
derivations.conditions: Applied to a ferrimagnetic crystal divided into two interpenetrating sublattices A and B with respective magnetizations M<sub>A</sub> and M<sub>B</sub>.
steps: Write the effective magnetic fields acting on sublattices A and B considering intra-sublattice and inter-sublattice molecular field coefficients: H<sub>A</sub> = H + λ<sub>AA</sub> M<sub>A</sub> + λ<sub>AB</sub> M<sub>B</sub> and H<sub>B</sub> = H + λ<sub>BA</sub> M<sub>A</sub> + λ<sub>BB</sub> M<sub>B</sub>, where λ<sub>AB</sub> = λ<sub>BA</sub>.

Apply the Curie law for each sublattice in the paramagnetic region (T > T<sub>N</sub>): M<sub>A</sub> = (C<sub>A</sub>/T) H<sub>A</sub> and M<sub>B</sub> = (C<sub>B</sub>/T) H<sub>B</sub>, where C<sub>A</sub> and C<sub>B</sub> are the Curie constants of sublattices A and B.
Express the equations in matrix form for M<sub>A</sub> and M<sub>B</sub> in terms of external magnetic field H, and solve for the total susceptibility χ = (M<sub>A</sub> + M<sub>B</sub>)/H.
Invert the resulting expression to obtain the reciprocal susceptibility equation showing hyperbolic temperature dependence.

derivations.title: Net Magnetic Moment per Formula Unit in Spinels
derivations.conditions: Assuming collinear alignment of spins on tetrahedral (A) and octahedral (B) sites in a 2-3 spinel ferrite.
steps: Identify the distribution of divalent and trivalent ions across A and B sites.
Sum the magnetic moments (in Bohr magnetons, μ<sub>B</sub>) for all ions residing on the B sites: μ<sub>B</sub> = ∑ μ<sub>B,i</sub>.
Sum the magnetic moments for all ions residing on the A sites: μ<sub>A</sub> = ∑ μ<sub>A,j</sub>.
Subtract the tetrahedral moment sum from the octahedral moment sum due to antiparallel alignment: μ<sub>net</sub> = |μ<sub>B</sub> - μ<sub>A</sub>|.

formula_sheet.variables: N_i = Number of magnetic ions per unit volume on sublattice i, g = Landé g-factor, S = Spin quantum number, k_B = Boltzmann constant

formula_sheet.variables: C = Total Curie constant, C_A and C_B = Sublattice constants

formula_sheet.conditions: Spontaneous net magnetization vanishes at T_{comp}

graphs_and_experiments.title: Inverse Magnetic Susceptibility vs Temperature
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of 1/χ on the vertical axis against temperature T on the horizontal axis, showing a linear asymptotic behavior at high temperatures that curves downward near T<sub>N</sub>, intersecting the temperature axis below T<sub>N</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the failure of the simple Curie-Weiss law and confirms negative inter-sublattice exchange interactions characteristic of ferrimagnetism.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Distinguishing ferrimagnetism from ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism in qualitative graphical multiple-choice questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Sublattice and Net Magnetization vs Temperature
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Curves for M<sub>A</sub>(T) and M<sub>B</sub>(T) decreasing with temperature and intersecting or dropping to zero at T<sub>N</sub>, alongside the resultant net magnetization curve M(T) = |M<sub>B</sub> - M<sub>A</sub>| which may show a compensation point.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how differing thermal coefficients of sublattice magnetizations can produce anomalous net magnetization curves, including compensation temperatures.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Explaining anomalous magnetic behavior in mixed ferrites (e.g., lithium ferrites).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Hysteresis Loop of a Ferrimagnetic Material
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A B-H or M-H loop characterized by high saturation magnetization (though lower than pure iron), moderate coercivity, and very high electrical resistivity.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows ferromagnetic-like saturation and remanence combined with low eddy current losses due to high resistance.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Core selection criteria for high-frequency transformer and memory device applications.

solved_numericals.question: A ferrimagnetic spinel has two sublattices A and B. The magnetic moment of ions on sublattice A is 3 μ<sub>B</sub> per formula unit pointing in one direction, and on sublattice B is 10 μ<sub>B</sub> per formula unit pointing in the opposite direction. Calculate the net magnetic moment per formula unit.
solution_steps: Apply the formula for net spontaneous magnetic moment: μ<sub>net</sub> = |μ<sub>B</sub> - μ<sub>A</sub>|.

solved_numericals.question: In a symmetric two-sublattice ferrimagnet, the Curie constants for sublattices A and B are equal (C<sub>A</sub> = C<sub>B</sub> = C/2). If the molecular field coefficient between sublattices is λ<sub>AB</sub> = -500 and the intra-sublattice coefficients are zero, estimate the Néel temperature T<sub>N</sub>.
solution_steps: Recall the relation for Néel temperature in a two-sublattice model: T_N = \frac{C}{2} |\lambda_{AB}|, where C = C_A + C_B.
Since C_A = C_B = C/2, the total Curie constant is C = C_A + C_B.
Substitute the parameter values into the expression to find T<sub>N</sub>.

solved_numericals.question: Consider a magnetite (Fe<sub>3</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) crystal treated as a ferrimagnet where Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions on A and B sites cancel out their moments, leaving the net moment entirely due to Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions on the B sites. If Fe<sup>2+</sup> has 4 unpaired electrons yielding a magnetic moment of 4 μ<sub>B</sub>, and there is 1 Fe<sup>2+</sup> ion per formula unit on B sites, what is the net moment per formula unit?
solution_steps: Identify the magnetic contribution from Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions: equal numbers on A and B sites pointing oppositely, resulting in zero net moment contribution (μ<sub>Fe3+</sub> = 0 net).
Identify the contribution from Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions: located on B sites with moment μ = 4 μ<sub>B</sub>.

assumptions_and_limitations: The molecular field approximation assumes that thermal fluctuations average out spatial variations in the local exchange field, which breaks down near absolute zero or in disordered systems.

The simple two-sublattice model assumes collinear spin alignments; however, complex ferrimagnets often exhibit canted spin structures (e.g., Yafet-Kittel triangular arrangements) at low temperatures or high fields.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Ferrimagnetism is identical to antiferromagnetism because adjacent spins are antiparallel.
common_misconceptions.correct: Ferrimagnetic sublattices have unequal magnetic moments, resulting in a net nonzero spontaneous magnetization, whereas antiferromagnetic sublattices have equal and opposite moments resulting in zero net magnetization.
common_misconceptions.why: The inequality in moment magnitudes or numbers per unit volume breaks complete cancellation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Ferrimagnetic materials have zero electrical resistance like metals.
common_misconceptions.correct: Most practical ferrimagnets (ferrites) are ceramic insulators or semiconductors with very high electrical resistivity.
common_misconceptions.why: Ionic bonding and localized d-electrons prevent free electron conduction, suppressing eddy current losses.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Above the Néel temperature, a ferrimagnet behaves according to the simple Curie law χ = C/T.
common_misconceptions.correct: Above T<sub>N</sub>, the inverse susceptibility follows a hyperbolic temperature dependence due to inter-sublattice interactions.
common_misconceptions.why: The coupling between different sublattices introduces non-linear temperature terms in the paramagnetic susceptibility.

quick_revision: Ferrimagnetism features antiparallel unequal magnetic moments giving a net spontaneous magnetization.
Common examples include spinels and magnetites (MO·Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>).
The transition temperature above which ferrimagnetism disappears is the Néel temperature (T<sub>N</sub>).
Paramagnetic susceptibility above T<sub>N</sub> deviates from the simple Curie-Weiss law, showing hyperbolic behavior.
High electrical resistivity makes ferrites indispensable for high-frequency transformer cores and microwave devices.
